<div class="lead">Benefits of Scrap 'n Ravel:</div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>        <ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>            <li>Use waste knitting to hang cast on comb and/or weights in place</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>            <li>Leave waste knitting in place to make blocking easier – especially for edges that roll</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>        </ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>    </div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>    <div class="col-sm-4 col-xs-12"> <img class="img-responsive zoom" code='0a'/>        <li>Work a fast cast on with waste yarn</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>        <li>Knit a few rows</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>        <li>Knit a row of ravel cord (so you can remove the scrap easily)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>        <li>Start knitting with the garment yarn, safely leaving open stitches to be worked later</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>    </ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>    You'll practice this in the next section.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="lead">What is End on the LEFT</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Knit 1 row with ravel cord.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Carriage on the right</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Starting on the left, with the garment yarn, e-wrap cast on over all the needles (over the ravel cord stitches)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Thread your carriage</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Continue knitting</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Drop the knitting from the machine</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ol><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><h3>Chain Cast On (with waste yarn)</h3><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ol class="instruction-list"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Cast on with waste yarn and ravel cord</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Starting on the left, follow the video</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Form a slip knot and place it on your latch tool</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Insert the tool between the first and second needle</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Catch the working yarn in the hook of the tool</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Pull the strand through the slip knot, forming a new loop.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Keeping the loop in the hook of the tool, position the tool between the next 2 needles.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Reach up and hook the working yarn again, pulling it through the loop on the hook. No guesswork.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="row"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-sm-6 col-xs-12 col-sm-offset-3"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class='embed-video-container'><iframe src='https://player.vimeo.com/video/343513501' frameborder='0' webkitAllowFullScreen mozallowfullscreen allowFullScreen></iframe></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></string></var><var name='EXCERCISE_TASK_5'><string><b>My Favorite Bind Off - Stitch thru Stitch</b></string></var><var name='EXCERCISE_DETAILS_2'><string>OK, if you are knitting a swatch and you are going to wash it, or you are going to handle your knitted piece a lot, Just leaving open stitches isn't practical you'll want to secure the stitches. <br><br> Running the tail of yarn through each stitch is a fast way to secure them.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="row"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>    <div class="col-sm-4 col-sm-offset-1 col-xs-6"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>        <div class='embed-video-container'><iframe src='https://player.vimeo.com/video/343495391' frameborder='0' webkitAllowFullScreen mozallowfullscreen allowFullScreen></iframe><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>        </div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>    </div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>        <div class="col-sm-5 col-sm-offset-1col-xs-6"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>            <i class="fa fa-lightbulb-o fa-2x" aria-hidden="true"></i> Sometimes you have a very stretchy, open piece of knitting. <wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>156</string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string><div class="row cleanwell"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-7"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><h4><strong>GAUGE SWATCH</strong></h4><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>The <strong>gauge swatch</strong> is the "official" swatch used when designing a garment.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>It is knit at a specific size, marked for accurate stitch and row measurement and "dressed" as the final garment will be treated.<br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><blockquote class="smallblock"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><em>TIP: Whatever method you use to create a swatch, the key is to correctly measure it and calculate your gauge.</em></blockquote></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-5"><img class="img-responsive" src="//www.knititnow.com/challenge/images/swatch_measure.jpg" /></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div></string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>58</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

<wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>58</string></var><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string><div class="row cleanwell"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-md-12 col-xs-12"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><h4><strong>TENSION SWATCH</strong></h4><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><em>When I pick up a new cone of yarn, I can't wait to thread up my machine and see what the yarn looks like.   From the initial cast on, I start guessing what setting on my tension dial I need to use.  I knit a few inches and reach down and start to feel the resulting fabric. <br /><br />Once I get a feel for the yarn (what machine, general tension setting at stockinette, etc) I create a<strong> tension swatch</strong>.  This helps me fine-tune the tension needed to achieve the fabric I like and allows me to play with various techniques.  <strong>I'm often very surprised that a yarn looks great in tuck, and awful in slip</strong>, for example.  Adding a few eyelets here and there tells me if the yarn will work up in lace.</em><br /> <br /> Let's practice knitting a <strong>tension swatch.</strong></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div></string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>258</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

<wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>4490</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>3308</string></var><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string><div class="row well"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-xs-12 col-md-10"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><h4>Play!</h4><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ol class="instruction-list"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Start knitting stockenette at the tightest tension that will knit.  (If the tension is too tight, you'll see stitches that don't form properly.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Knit 2-4 inches. I'm often very pleasantly surprised at the result.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Transfer every other needle to out of work postion and knit a section - put all needles back into work.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Work a simple tuck, or slip, or any stitch pattern of your choice ... base your tension dial setting on the stockinette sections you just knit.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ol><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><blockquote class="smallblock">The point of this exercise is to put the yarn through it's paces ... ignite your creativity, and get a feel for what the yarn can do.  If you don't have a huge cone, you can always re-wind this knitting. <wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>3473</string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>4891</string></var><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string><div class="row"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-sm-6 col-xs-12"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><h3>Knitting a “Proper” Swatch</h3><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>The goal of a swatch is to determine how many stitches and rows it takes to knit a 1” (or 4”/10cm) square.<br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>To do this accurately, you will knit a larger piece, and mark of a set number of stitches and rows AS YOU KNIT.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>After you dress (rest, wash, block) your swatch, you can easily measure and calculate your stitch and row gauge.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>When you knit your swatch, you will cast on MORE stitches and knit MORE rows than shown.  This will prevent you from measuring edge to edge and ONLY MEASURE the ISOLATED AREA.<br><br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ol class="instruction-list"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Garment yarn: Cast on 50 stitches with any method</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li> Knit for 1” or so - carriage on the right</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Contrasting waste yarn: Knit 2 rows</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li> Garment yarn: knit 20 rows</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Use a yarn marker or run a strand as you knit, isolate the stitches.</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li> Knit 20 rows</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Contrasting waste yarn: Knit 2 rows</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Garment yarn: knit 1” or so</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li> Bind off or drop the work from the machine</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li> Dress the swatch (wash, block and treat as you will the finished item)</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ol><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-sm-4 col-xs-12"><img class="img-responsive" src="/challenge/images/v2/50/lk-150_swatch2.png"></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

BlockTitle: Knit 'n Purl Stitches on the Machine
details: <wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>3503</string></var><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string><div class="row"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-sm-6 col-xs-12"><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>One of the first surprises for most machine knitters is the fact that the humble garter stitch is problematic on the knitting machine. Because our needles face in one direction and they form uniform stitches in one direction, we can easily produce stockinette stitch (translated knit 1 row, purl 1 row) but to knit every row?…..<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Be default, knitting machines knit stockinette stitch. Stockinette has a smooth side (knit) side and a bumpy side (purl side)<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>In hand knitting terms this is knit 1 row purl 1 row.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Hand knitters can easily knit garter stitch by knitting every row. The "purl bumps" are visible on both sides of the knitting.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>As machine knitters we have to take steps to show the purl bumps on the opposite side of our knitting.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>There are a number of techniques you can use to get garter stitch texture in your knitting.<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Hand manipulate (re-form) stitches</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Removing live stitches from the machine, turning the work and rehanging the stitches</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>With a little planning machine knitters CAN incorporate purl bumps in our knitting.<br><br><em><small>You may have heard about an accessory called a RIBBER<a href="#" data-toggle="tooltip" data-placement="auto" title="A ribber is basically a second needlebed, positioned directly opposite the main bed. Because the needles face the opposite direction, both purl stitches and knit stitches can be formed "> <sup><i class="fa fa-question-circle-o" aria-hidden="true"></i></a></sup> for knitting machines.  The LK-150 was never designed with a ribber</small></em><br><center><a class="btn btn-primary" href="/classrooms/116/garter-stitch-on-the-machine" target="_new" role="button">Visit the Garter Stitch Classroom</a></center><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='09'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><div class="col-sm-4 col-xs-12"><img class="img-thumbnail" src="/challenge/images/v2/51/garter.jpg"></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></div><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>4972</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>

<wddxPacket version='1.0'><header/><data><struct ><var name='HTMLCONTENT'><string>Because the needles on our needlebeds are positioned in one direction, passing the carriage and knitting a row produces stitches with the purl bumps facing.<br><br><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>You might want purl bumps on the opposite side of the knitting:<char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Ribbing</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Garter stitch accent rows</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Vertical accents between cables</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Accents to eyelets for lace</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><b>To reform individual Stitches:</b><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><ol><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Use your latch tool to remove an individual stitch from the machine needle</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Insert the hook of the latch tool in the stitch in the row below</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Release the loose stitch</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Place the stitch behind the latch</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Place the unknit strand in the hook of the tool</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Pull the strand through, closing the latch with the stitch and forming a new stitch</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/>Replace the new stitch back on the machine</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><li>Notice that the purl bump is now away from you</li><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></ul><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/><char code='0d'/><char code='0a'/></string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID'><string>3521</string></var><var name='FIELDNAMES'><string>CHALLENGE_ASSIGNID,CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID,HTMLCONTENT</string></var><var name='CHALLENGE_COMPONENTID'><string>5015</string></var></struct></data></wddxPacket>
